title: Integrated Security & Compliance Playbook — RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, and Evidence Workflows
author: Natalie Rivera
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's operational controls and procedures for role-based access control (RBAC), authentication and provisioning, centralized audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) gates, incident response for security incidents, compliance evidence collection, and the risk & exceptions process. It is a reference for security, engineering, SRE, product, and compliance teams.

Scope: Applies to all Redwood-hosted services, the control plane used in Dedicated and Private deployments, developer tools, and infrastructure components that store or process customer data. Exceptions for strictly on-prem packages are documented in the risk & exceptions section.

Owners and escalation
- Document owner: Security (security@redwood.com) — primary contact: Natalie Rivera (CISO office).
- Oncall & escalation: security-oncall@redwood.com, eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com.
- Evidence & audit requests: security-compliance@redwood.com.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Executive summary: We maintain a principle of least privilege with clearly defined roles, automated provisioning via SSO/SCIM, and regular access reviews. Privileged operations require MFA and just-in-time elevation where possible.

Roles (baseline):
- org-admin — full organization-level administration, reserved for senior ops & security engineers (limit to ~5 people in production).
- security-admin — manage security config, evidence workflows, and incident coordination.
- infra-admin — cloud and infra administration (IAM, VPC, compute).
- svc-account — non-human service identities; scoped by least privilege and bound by expiry policies.
- developer — standard engineering access to development environments and CI/CD; no production secret access by default.
- read-only — limited access for auditing and reporting.
- compliance-audit — restricted view to audit logs, policy documents, and evidence packages.

Authentication and provisioning:
- Primary identity provider: Okta (SAML 2.0) with SCIM for automated provisioning and deprovisioning to GitHub, GCP/AWS, and internal admin consoles.
- Alternative: Azure AD (SAML/OIDC) for enterprise customers using Private deployments.
- MFA: Required for all human accounts; hardware MFA (U2F/WebAuthn) required for org-admin and infra-admin roles.
- Service tokens: Short-lived (max 90 days) and rotated per pipeline. Long-lived tokens require documented justification and CISO approval.
- Just-in-time (JIT) elevation: Audit-tracked elevation for privileged tasks via admin-bastion or ephemeral role grants.

Access reviews and attestations:
- Quarterly access review for org-admin and infra-admin roles (owner: security).
- Monthly automated inactive account report (remove accounts inactive > 60 days).
- SCIM deprovisioning must complete within 2 hours of directory disable.

2) Audit logging

Goals: Capture sufficient telemetry to support incident investigations, compliance attestations, and anomaly detection while minimizing collection of customer-sensitive payloads.

Log sources (examples):
- Control plane: auth events, policy changes, RBAC grants, role-elevations.
- Serving runtime: inference request metadata (request ID, customer ID, model used, latency, token counts) — payloads are NOT logged by default for hosted customers.
- Infrastructure: instance lifecycle, network flow logs, KMS usage, storage access events.
- CI/CD and code repo events: deployments, release tags, image promotions.
- Administrative console: policy edits, billing exports, and audit exports.

Log schema (example fields): timestamp, service, namespace, event_type, actor_id, actor_role, target_resource, action, request_id, correlation_id, result, source_ip, user_agent. (PII/PHI fields are explicitly excluded unless customer opts in with a documented retention policy.)

Retention & storage:
- Hot retention (queryable): 365 days in Elasticsearch/Opensearch for security investigations and analytics.
- Cold retention (archival): 7 years in WORM S3 archive for compliance evidence (encrypted at rest, access audited).
- Short-term retention for debug-only environments: 30 days configurable per environment.

Access and controls:
- Only members of compliance-audit and security-admin groups can export raw logs to external storage.
- Exports require an evidence request and are tracked with an export ticket ID.
- Audit log access is logged and subject to monthly review.

Alerting & detection thresholds (examples):
- Authentication: > 10 failed login attempts for a single principal within 5 minutes triggers a priority P1 alert.
- Unusual RBAC change: org-admin grant outside regular business hours triggers a P2 review alert.
- Data exfil indicators: any bulk export of customer data > 1GB within 24 hours triggers immediate investigation.

Example CLI query (Opensearch):
- curl -XPOST "https://opensearch.internal/_search" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":{"bool":{"must":[{"term":{"event_type":"auth.login"}},{"range":{"@timestamp":{"gte":"now-1h"}}}]}}}'

3) Data residency & retention

Principles:
- Customers can choose regionally-isolated deployments (US, EU, APAC) for hosted and Dedicated. Private deployments keep all data within the customer-managed network.
- Default policy avoids logging or storing full request payloads. When payloads are required for debugging, collection is opt-in or gated via approval.

Default retention tables (hosted):
- Authentication & metadata logs: 365 days (hot) / 7 years (archive).
- Inference request metadata: 90 days (hot); payloads not stored by default.
- Embeddings / vector indexes: customer-configurable; default retention 30 days for ephemeral embeddings used for cache/optimization.
- Billing & usage records: 7 years (for accounting).

Customer opt-in / regulated customers:
- For regulated customers (e.g., finance, healthcare), retention and residency are configured per contract and documented in the customer's security profile.
- On-prem/Private: data deletion SLA handled by the customer; Redwood provides tools and playbooks for safe deletion and verification.

Data deletion SLA (hosted):
- Standard delete request: processed within 30 days, confirmation provided with deletion proof (manifest of affected resources and a verified purge timestamp).
- Emergency deletion (legal order or breach): processed within 72 hours; security & legal expedite the process.

Encryption & key management:
- Data at rest: AES-256. All production buckets are encrypted using KMS-managed keys.
- KMS integration: customer-managed keys (BYOK) supported for Dedicated and Private.
- Key rotation: platform keys rotated annually; customer-managed keys follow the customer's KMS policy.

4) Secure SDLC (DevSecOps gates)

Overview: Security is embedded across the product lifecycle: design, build, test, deploy, and operate. Required artifacts are captured in PR templates, deployment manifests, and release checklists.

Required controls per change: 
- Threat modeling: required for changes affecting authentication, data flows, or infra boundary changes; owner: proposer + security reviewer.
- Static analysis & SCA: run on every PR. High-severity findings must be resolved before merge.
- Dependency policy: no use of packages with known critical CVEs; auto-block via dependency scanner.
- Container image signing: signed images from the build pipeline; SBOM generated and attached to release.
- Secrets scanning: integrated in CI; failed scan blocks merge.
- Security approval: changes touching infra or prod config require one security approver + one owner approver.
- Pre-deploy canary: run canary for at least 1 hour or 1000 requests (whichever comes first) for model-serving changes. Canary rollback triggers: error rate increase > 1% absolute or 50% relative latency regression.

Developer responsibilities:
- Use documented secure coding patterns (internal link to secure-coding-guidelines).
- Add unit and integration tests to validate input sanitation and access checks.
- Provide a short risk assessment in PR description when relevant.

5) Incident response — security-specific procedures

Classification & severity:
- Sev-S1 (Security Incident): confirmed compromise of production credentials, data exfiltration, or persistent attacker presence. Target initial response: 1 hour.
- Sev-S2 (High): unauthorized access without confirmed exfiltration, privilege escalation attempts. Target initial response: 4 hours.
- Sev-S3 (Medium): suspicious activity requiring investigation (failed scans, anomalous configuration changes).

Key runbook steps (quick reference):
1. Triage & contain — collect ephemeral evidence (memory, process lists) and isolate affected hosts/services. Owner: security-oncall + incident commander.
2. Preserve evidence — create forensic snapshots; ensure WORM archival of relevant audit logs and preserve chain-of-custody.
3. Eradicate & remediate — rotate impacted credentials, patch affected images, revoke tokens, remove malicious artifacts.
4. Recovery — restore services from trusted images, run post-recovery validation tests, and resume traffic with monitoring.
5. Post-incident analysis — produce a security postmortem, root cause analysis, and mitigations. Target: preliminary report within 72 hours; final postmortem within 30 days.

Communication & regulatory handling:
- Customer notification: follow contract terms and notification SLAs. Legal and customer success draft notifications; security provides technical summary and evidence package.
- Regulators / law enforcement: route all external disclosures through Legal. For cross-border data incidents, coordinate with Privacy and Compliance for notification obligations.

Forensic preservation checklist (minimum):
- Timestamps of detection, initial triage logs, affected resource list, copies of relevant audit logs, network flow captures, process/packet captures if available, and image hashes of suspicious binaries.

6) Compliance evidence workflows

Purpose: Standardize collection and packaging of artifacts required for audits (SOC2, ISO27001, contractual audits).

Evidence package contents (typical):
- RBAC roster: list of active role assignments and recent access review attestations.
- Audit logs: filtered set corresponding to scope (time window + services).
- Config snapshots: infrastructure-as-code manifests, VPC/network configs, KMS key policy.
- SDLC artifacts: PR approvals, SCA findings, SBOM, image signatures.
- Pen test & assessment reports: recent penetration test executive summary and remediation timeline.
- Policy documents: retention, encryption, privacy policies and exceptions.

Workflow steps:
1. Request intake — compliance auditor or customer sends evidence request to security-compliance@redwood.com with scope and timeframe.
2. Triage & assignment — security assigns evidence owner and creates collection ticket with a due date (standard SLA: 10 business days).
3. Collection — owners gather RBAC exports, signed logs, config snapshots, and any supporting runbooks.
4. Review & redact — security reviews package; redact any customer-sensitive payloads that exceed scope.
5. Deliver & log — deliver the package via secure transfer (SFTP or signed download link) and log delivery in the Evidence Tracker.
6. Retain delivery proof — store a copy of the delivered package in the archival evidence bucket with access audit.

SLA & escalation:
- Standard evidence requests: 10 business days. Expedited: 3 business days with approval from the CISO.
- Missed SLA: automatically escalated to Head of Security and VP of Product.

Example evidence CSV headers: request_id, delivered_at, owner, items_included, access_restrictions, export_ticket_id

7) Risk & exceptions process

When a control cannot be implemented immediately, teams must request a documented exception. Exceptions are time-limited and require compensating controls.

Exception request requirements:
- Description of the gap and business justification.
- Risk assessment (likelihood x impact) and proposed compensating controls.
- Proposed expiration date (max 90 days by default).
- Responsible owner for mitigation and monitoring.

Approval path:
- Low-risk exceptions: Security Manager sign-off.
- Medium/high: Security Director + CISO.
- Any exception impacting customer data residency, auditability, or encryption requires CISO + Legal approval.

Monitoring & review:
- Approved exceptions appear in the risk register and are reviewed weekly until mitigated.
- Expired exceptions must either be remediated immediately or re-approved with updated mitigations.

8) Operational checklists & runbooks (quick links)

- Quarterly RBAC review checklist: export role assignments, confirm 2 approvers for privilege roles, record attestation.
- Audit log export runbook: steps to create an export ticket, snapshot query, encrypt export, and upload to evidence bucket.
- Incident evidence preservation runbook: preserve logs, image hashes, and initiate WORM archival.
- Data deletion verification: steps to verify purge across S3, indices, backups, and caches.

9) Metrics & reporting

Key metrics maintained by security & SRE:
- Mean time to detect (MTTD) security incidents (target: < 1 hour for Sev-S1).
- Mean time to contain (MTTC) (target: < 4 hours for Sev-S1).
- % of privileged accounts reviewed per quarter (target: 100% for org-admin & infra-admin).
- Evidence request SLA compliance (target: 95% within 10 business days).

Appendix A — Contact matrix
- Security Oncall: security-oncall@redwood.com (primary).
- Security Compliance: security-compliance@redwood.com.
- SRE Oncall: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com.

Appendix B — Change history
- 2026-11-02: Initial published playbook (Natalie Rivera).
- 2027-03-15: Added JIT elevation guidance and updated audit retention to 365 days hot / 7 years archive (reviewer: Samir Patel).
- 2027-12-01: Incorporated evidence SLA and expanded incident forensic checklist (reviewers: Linh Tran, Carlos Mendez).

Notes and references: links to internal runbooks and external standards are included where appropriate: SOC2 control mappings, ISO27001 clauses, and data-protection guidance (GDPR). For operational procedures, follow the runbooks linked under the security-and-compliance space.

If you are implementing or relying on a control in this document and need clarification, contact security@redwood.com.
